_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to use quartiles, interquartile range and boxplots to compare data distributions.

_source.w: We are learning to use quartiles, interquartile range and boxplots to compare data distributions.
y: Boxplots provide a powerful visual summary of a dataset's centre, spread and skewness using five key values.
The interquartile range is resistant to outliers, making it a more reliable measure of spread than range for many datasets.
These tools are used throughout science, medicine, business and social research to compare distributions.
eg: Constructing a boxplot from a dataset and identifying the median, quartiles and any outliers.
Comparing two boxplots side by side and discussing differences in centre, spread and skewness.
Calculating the IQR and using it to identify outliers (values beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles).
Interpreting: 'The median score for Year 10 is higher than Year 9, but Year 9 has a wider IQR.'
Drawing parallel boxplots to compare the distributions of test scores for three different classes.
Discussing when boxplots are more informative than histograms and vice versa.

toLevel2.question: The median is the most frequently occurring value when data is arranged in order.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The median is the middle value, not the most frequent. The most frequently occurring value is the mode.

distractors.explanation: The median is the middle value in an ordered data set, not the most frequent.

toLevel2.question: The interquartile range is calculated as Q1 minus Q3.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1, not Q1 − Q3. Subtracting in the wrong order gives a negative value.

distractors.explanation: Subtracting Q3 from Q1 gives the spread of the middle 50%.

toLevel2.question: A boxplot displays the five-number summary of a data set.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A boxplot shows the minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum (or outlier boundaries).

distractors.explanation: A boxplot only shows the mean and standard deviation.

toLevel2.question: The IQR measures the spread of the entire data set.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The IQR measures the spread of only the middle 50% of data, from Q1 to Q3.

distractors.explanation: IQR captures all data values from minimum to maximum.

toLevel2.question: In a boxplot, the box contains exactly 50% of the data.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The box spans from Q1 to Q3, which by definition contains the middle 50% of data.

distractors.explanation: The box contains 25% of the data, with the rest in the whiskers.

toLevel2.question: A wider box in a boxplot means more data values than a narrower box.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A wider box indicates greater spread in the middle 50%, not more data. Both boxes contain 50% of their data.

distractors.explanation: More data is contained in wider boxes because they cover more values.

toLevel2.question: Q1 is the median of the lower half of the data.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Q1 (first quartile) is found by taking the median of all values below the overall median.

distractors.explanation: Q1 is the smallest value in the data set.

toLevel2.question: A data point is always classified as an outlier if it is the largest value.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The largest value is only an outlier if it exceeds Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Being the largest does not automatically make it an outlier.

distractors.explanation: The maximum value in any data set is always an outlier.

toLevel2.question: The five-number summary consists of the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: These five values summarise the centre, spread, and range of a data set.
